newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania exodus picks up, food crisis looms.
newsitem.headline: Albania exodus picks up, food crisis looms.

text.p: The pace of the refugee exodus from Albania picked up on Tuesday as people desperate to leave their anarchic country crowded into anything that floated and paddled or sailed out to sea.

The Albanian government appealed to a visiting European Union mission for urgent financial aid to get the country back on its feet after weeks of unrest, saying it was facing a serious food crisis after government grain stocks were looted.
An alliance of 11 political parties repeated an appeal for President Sali Berisha to resign as the best way of restoring order in Europe's poorest country.

Rebels who seized arms and took control of southern Albania in fury, blaming the government for a string of investment scheme collapses, say that unless Berisha quits by March 20 they will elect their own presidential council to challenge him directly.
They also said they had urged the government of Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, who is expected to visit the south on Wednesday to talk to rebel leaders, to cut all ties with Berisha.

Parliamentary speaker Pjeter Arbnori described the ultimatum as an attempt to destabilise the country and called for all political parties to observe an agreement on national reconciliation signed with Berisha last week.
The situation in the capital Tirana was returning to normal, though a state of emergency and night curfew remained.
The government said the airport, closed since last week, would reopen on Thursday. It was not immediately clear whether international airlines would resume flights immediately.
On Albania's Adriatic coast, there were more chaotic scenes as hundreds of would-be refugees clambered aboard rusting hulks without motors and drifted out to sea.
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said more than 2,500 people fled to Italy on Tuesday, more than on any single day to date, adding to nearly 10,000 who had already reached Italy and Greece.

In Durres, Albania's main port 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, nearly 100 people took a derelict freighter out of the harbour, using makeshift paddles, sails fashioned from garbage bags and the current.
The ship ran aground south of Durres and the passengers were brought back to shore by motorised rubber dinghies.
The chaos prompted marine insurance writers in London effectively to declare the area a war zone liable to increased premiums.
On the other side of the Adriatic in the southern Italian port of Brindisi, refugees spoke of paying up to $600 per head to get out of Albania.

"I paid and I would pay again if I had to," said a 28-year-old businessman who handed over the equivalent of $3,000 for his five-strong family, while another man said he had sold his house and car to pay the passage.
Concern was mounting in Italy that it could be facing a tide of illegal immigration and crime rather than a genuine refugee crisis.

Italy's chief anti-Mafia prosecutor, Pier Luigi Vigna, said he feared that the exodus might include criminals released by the government for their own safety during the armed anarchy that swept Albania.
In Tirana, Finance Minister Arben Malaj told a news conference he had asked the visiting EU delegation for financial aid. He declined to give a figure but said it had "shocked" delegation members.

He said urgent action was needed to restore financial institutions and secure the ports, adding: "If we fail to take such steps, then I'm very pessimistic about our capacity to normalise the situation and enable foreign institutions to help us."
